clinicalPearls: A rare, usually unilateral congenital anomaly in which a deep, sharply demarcated fundus excavation surrounds a relatively normal-appearing optic disc at its base.
The disc lies at the bottom of the excavation and, unlike the morning glory anomaly, shows no central glial tuft and no anomalous radial vessels.
The walls of the excavation show atrophic changes of the retinal pigment epithelium and choroid.
Usually non-progressive and typically not associated with the multisystem or midline anomalies seen with morning glory disc.
Vision is variable; acuity may be reduced with associated field defects, though some eyes see relatively well.
Differentiation from morning glory anomaly and optic disc coloboma rests on the near-normal disc morphology at the base of a peripapillary excavation.
Occasionally complicated by serous macular detachment or contractile movements of the excavation.
Distinguished from acquired peripapillary excavations of pathological myopia by its congenital, stationary nature.
reference.pathophysiology: Peripapillary staphyloma is thought to arise from a congenital defect in the differentiation and development of the peripapillary sclera and choroid, with deficient or attenuated tissue in the region immediately surrounding the optic nerve head. This weakness allows the peripapillary structures to bow posteriorly, producing a deep excavation whose walls display retinal pigment epithelial and choroidal atrophy while the optic disc at the base remains comparatively spared. Unlike the morning glory anomaly, there is no primary mesodermal glial dysgenesis at the disc itself, which accounts for the relatively normal disc appearance. The distorted peripapillary geometry accounts for the visual field changes and predisposition to secondary serous retinal changes.
additionalDifferentials: Posterior scleral ectasia of other cause
additionalInvestigations: Dilated fundus examination and fundus photography
Optical coherence tomography of the disc and peripapillary region
B-scan ultrasonography to demonstrate posterior scleral excavation
MRI or CT of the orbit where posterior segment anatomy is unclear
Automated perimetry to characterise the field defect
Serial imaging to confirm the stationary, non-progressive nature
redFlags: New central distortion suggesting a serous macular detachment
Progressive excavation, which is atypical and should prompt reassessment
Bilateral involvement or associated ocular malformations
Reduced acuity with a relative afferent pupillary defect indicating significant nerve involvement
reference.prognosis: The anomaly is generally stationary with a stable, if variable, visual outcome; many eyes retain useful vision. Rare secondary complications such as serous macular detachment can reduce central acuity.
pitfalls: Confusing peripapillary staphyloma with the morning glory anomaly, which carries very different systemic implications.
Mislabelling a congenital excavation as glaucomatous cupping and initiating pressure-lowering therapy unnecessarily.
Overlooking a superimposed serous macular detachment as the cause of new visual symptoms.
Failing to distinguish it from acquired myopic staphyloma, leading to incorrect prognostic counselling.
references: Kanski's Clinical Ophthalmology: A Systematic Approach
American Academy of Ophthalmology Basic and Clinical Science Course, Pediatric Ophthalmology and Strabismus
management: Manage conservatively, as this congenital anomaly is usually stationary and non-progressive with no disease-specific therapy
Correct any refractive error and optimise vision in the affected eye, with amblyopia therapy in children
Monitor with serial dilated fundus examination, optical coherence tomography and automated perimetry to characterise field defects and confirm stability
Detect and treat secondary complications such as serous macular or retinal detachment promptly to preserve central acuity
Distinguish it from morning glory anomaly and optic disc coloboma so that associated systemic or midline anomalies are appropriately excluded
Refer to ophthalmology, including paediatric ophthalmology in children, for ongoing surveillance and visual rehabilitation
